entry: American daily [[Newspaper|newspaper]] based in [[Manhattan]], New York City. Founded in 1851 as the New-York Daily Times, it is one of the longest-running newspapers in the U.S. and one of the country's newspapers of record. The company that publishes it has been chaired by the Ochs-Sulzberger family since 1896. In 1971 the paper published the Pentagon Papers, an internal Department of Defense document detailing U.S. involvement in the [[Vietnam War]], despite pushback from then-president [[Richard Nixon]]; the Supreme Court ruled that the First Amendment guaranteed the right to publish them. The paper has won the [[Pulitzer Prize]] 135 times since 1918, the most of any publication. As of June 2026 it had 13.35 million total subscribers, the highest number of any U.S. newspaper. Critics have argued that its coverage shows a liberal bias.

1642 painting by [[Rembrandt|Rembrandt van Rijn]], completed at the peak of the [[Dutch Golden Age]]. It depicts the Militia Company of District II moving out under Captain Frans Banninck Cocq and his lieutenant, Willem van Ruytenburch. Rembrandt transformed a conventional group portrait of a civic militia into a dramatic scene energized by light and shadow. The painting was commissioned around 1639 by Cocq and seventeen members of his guard, and Rembrandt was paid 1,600 guilders for it. The title is a misnomer, since the scene is not nocturnal. In 1715 the painting was trimmed on all four sides to fit between columns in the [[Amsterdam]] Town Hall, which removed two figures and part of the arch. It is now displayed in the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Hidden in a cave during [[World War II]] for protection, it has undergone over 25 restorations.

American rapper and songwriter from [[Brooklyn]], New York City, known as Biggie Smalls. A leading figure of East Coast [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]], he became in 1993 the first artist to sign with [[Sean Combs]]'s Bad Boy Records. His debut album, *Ready to Die* (1994), received acclaim. Following a feud with [[Tupac Shakur]], he was killed in a drive-by shooting in [[Los Angeles]] six months after Shakur's murder. His posthumous album *Life After Death* (1997) debuted atop the Billboard 200. Certified U.S. sales exceed 28 million copies. Inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2020.

1892 two-act [[Ballet|classical ballet]] by [[Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky]], set on Christmas Eve. Adapted from [[Alexandre Dumas]]'s short story *The Tale of a Nutcracker*, itself a retelling of E. T. A. Hoffmann's 1816 story, it follows a child who dreams of a nutcracker doll. [[Marius Petipa]] was the first choreographer, although Lev Ivanov is often credited. The ballet premiered with Tchaikovsky's opera *Iolanta* on December 18, 1892, in Saint Petersburg, Russia, and was not initially successful. Since the late 1960s many companies have danced it, especially in North America, where major American companies generate around 40% of their annual ticket revenues from it. The score, which uses the celesta, has become one of Tchaikovsky's most famous compositions.

American mockumentary [[Sitcom|sitcom]] (2005–2013). Adapted for [[NBC]] by Greg Daniels from the British series by [[Ricky Gervais]] and Stephen Merchant, it follows employees of the Dunder Mifflin Paper Company in Scranton, Pennsylvania. Its nine seasons comprised 201 episodes. [[Steve Carell]] starred as the regional manager in its most acclaimed seasons, which won five Primetime Emmy Awards, including Outstanding Comedy Series in 2006. Critics faulted the eighth season, after Carell's departure in season seven. In 2016 [[Rolling Stone]] named it one of the 100 greatest television shows of all time.

headword: The Old Man and the Sea
entry: 1952 novella by [[Ernest Hemingway]]. Its protagonist, Santiago, is an aging [[Cuba|Cuban]] fisherman who has gone 84 days without a catch when he hooks a giant [[Marlin|marlin]] far out in the [[Gulf Stream]]. Sharks devour much of the fish during his return. Hemingway wrote the 26,531-word manuscript in six weeks, between December 1950 and February 1951, and *Life* magazine published the full novella in its September 1, 1952, issue. It was the last major fictional work Hemingway published in his lifetime. In 1953 it won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction, and it was the only work explicitly mentioned when he received the 1954 Nobel Prize in Literature. Scholars continue to debate whether it is inferior or equal to his other works.

1967 coming-of-age novel by S. E. Hinton. Set in [[Tulsa, Oklahoma]], it follows Ponyboy Curtis, a teenager in a [[Gang|gang]] of working-class greasers who fights the wealthier Socs. Hinton published it under her initials so that male reviewers would not dismiss it because of her gender. A 1983 film directed by [[Francis Ford Coppola]] adapted it. A Tony Award-winning stage musical premiered in [[San Diego]] in 2023 and opened on Broadway in 2024. The novel has sold over eight million copies.

Headquarters of the [[United States Department of Defense|U.S. Department of Defense]] in Arlington County, [[Virginia]], across the Potomac River from [[Washington, D.C.]] Built on an accelerated schedule during [[World War II]] and dedicated on January 15, 1943, it is the world's second-largest office building, with about 6.5 million square feet of floor space. On September 11, 2001, five [[Al-Qaeda|al-Qaeda]] hijackers flew American Airlines Flight 77 into its western side, killing themselves and 184 others. It was the first significant foreign attack on federal facilities in the capital area since the Burning of Washington during the [[War of 1812]].

1931 painting by [[Salvador Dalí]], regarded as his most famous work and one of the most recognizable works of [[Surrealism]]. It was first exhibited at the Julien Levy Gallery in 1932 and sold for $250. In 1934 an anonymous donor gave it to the [[Museum of Modern Art]] in [[New York City]], where it has remained. Limp watches drape over a barren [[Catalonia|Catalan]] landscape, and a distorted profile face at the center approximates Dalí's own face. Dalí said the soft watches were not inspired by [[Special relativity|relativity]] theory but by a Camembert melting in the sun. The central creature is believed to have been modeled on a figure from [[Hieronymus Bosch]]'s *The Garden of Earthly Delights*. It is sometimes called "The Melting Clocks."

1986 musical by [[Andrew Lloyd Webber]], with lyrics by Charles Hart and Richard Stilgoe. Based on Gaston Leroux's 1910 novel, it tells of the soprano Christine Daaé and her obsession with a disfigured musical genius who lives beneath the [[Paris]] Opera House. The musical opened in London's West End in 1986 and on Broadway in 1988, winning the Olivier Award and the Tony Award for Best Musical. The Broadway production celebrated its 10,000th performance on February 11, 2012, and was the longest-running show in Broadway history. It is the second-longest-running West End musical, after [[Les Misérables (musical)|Les Misérables]]. The original London production closed in March 2020 because of the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] and reopened in a scaled-down staging in July 2021.

1910 [[Gothic fiction|Gothic horror]] novel by French author Gaston Leroux. Serialized in *Le Gaulois* from September 23, 1909, to January 8, 1910, it was partly inspired by events at the [[Paris]] Opera, including a fire that led to a chandelier crash killing one person. The underground lake in the novel is an actual [[Cistern|cistern]] beneath the opera house, still used to train firefighters. Its best-known adaptations are a 1925 film with Lon Chaney and [[Andrew Lloyd Webber]]'s 1986 musical.

1890 philosophical fiction and Gothic horror [[Novel|novel]] by Irish author [[Oscar Wilde]], his only novel. Basil Hallward, an artist infatuated with Dorian's beauty, paints his portrait, and Dorian is drawn into the [[Hedonism|hedonistic]] worldview of Lord Henry Wotton. Dorian sells his soul so that the portrait, rather than he himself, will age, and the portrait records every sin of his libertine life. The story first appeared in *Lippincott's Monthly Magazine* in July 1890, and the novel-length version was published in April 1891. Before publication an editor removed around five hundred words, including passages alluding to homosexuality. The book drew significant criticism, but it is now one of Wilde's best-known works. [[The Guardian]] listed it among the 100 best novels ever written in English.

Media franchise of comedy-mystery films and animated cartoons. Its films center on the inept French detective Inspector Jacques Clouseau, first played by [[Peter Sellers]]. The title refers to a large [[Diamond|pink diamond]] whose flaw resembles a leaping panther. The animated character debuted in the opening credits of *The Pink Panther* (1963), and its cartoons began with *The Pink Phink* (1964), which won an Academy Award. After Sellers's death in 1980 the series paused until reboots with [[Steve Martin]] in 2006 and 2009. In July 2025 [[Amazon (company)|Amazon]] MGM Studios announced a live-action reboot starring [[Eddie Murphy]].

English rock band formed in [[London]] in 1977. Its core members were [[Sting (musician)|Sting]], Andy Summers and Stewart Copeland. Emerging from the British [[Punk rock|punk]] scene, it moved into new wave and [[Reggae|reggae]] rock. Its album *Synchronicity* (1983) was number one in the UK, Canada, Australia, Italy and the U.S., and its single "Every Breath You Take" was its only U.S. number one. The Police disbanded in 1984 at the height of their fame and reunited in 2007 for a tour that was the year's highest-grossing. The band was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2003.

16th-century political treatise by Italian diplomat and political philosopher [[Niccolò Machiavelli]], written as an instruction guide for new princes. Its worldview treats practical effect as more important than any abstract ideal, and it includes positive references to the career of [[Cesare Borgia]]. Many commentators view immoral acts as sometimes necessary to achieve political glory. Printed in 1532, five years after Machiavelli's death, it is dedicated to [[Lorenzo de' Medici]], Duke of Urbino. It is sometimes claimed to be one of the first works of modern political philosophy, and it conflicted with the dominant Catholic and scholastic doctrines of its time. It is the most remembered of Machiavelli's works and the source of the pejorative "Machiavellian."

English [[Electronic music|electronic]] rave group formed in Braintree, [[Essex]], in 1990 around producer Liam Howlett. Pioneers of big beat, the band achieved early success with the singles "Charly" and "Everybody in the Place" in 1991. Its album *The Fat of the Land* (1997) went to number one in 16 countries, and its singles "Firestarter" and "Breathe" were UK number ones. The band has sold an estimated 25 million records worldwide. After Keith Flint's death, Howlett and Maxim continued the band. The Prodigy won three [[MTV]] Video Music Awards.

headword: The Protocols of the Elders of Zion
entry: [[Antisemitism|Antisemitic]] hoax and forgery purporting to detail a Jewish plot for global domination. Largely plagiarized from earlier sources, it was first published in [[Russian Empire|Imperial Russia]] in 1903. It helped popularize belief in an international Jewish [[Conspiracy theory|conspiracy]]. The British newspaper [[The Times]] exposed it as a forgery in 1921, and the German newspaper Frankfurter Zeitung did so in 1924. From 1933 German teachers assigned distillations of it to schoolchildren throughout [[Nazi Germany]] as if factual. Some antisemitic groups still present it as genuine. It has been described as "probably the most influential work of antisemitism ever written."

Narrative poem by American writer [[Edgar Allan Poe]], first published in January 1845. A distraught lover, often identified as a [[Student|student]], mourns the loss of Lenore when a raven visits him and repeatedly says "nevermore." Poe stated that he composed the poem in a logical and methodical manner, as he elaborated in his 1846 essay "The Philosophy of Composition." The poem was partly inspired by a talking raven in [[Charles Dickens]]'s 1841 novel *Barnaby Rudge*. It was first attributed to Poe in print in the *New York Evening Mirror* on January 29, 1845, and made him popular in his lifetime, though it brought him little financial success. The poem is often noted for its musicality and internal rhyme, and critical opinion on its literary status remains divided.

1989 novel by Nobel Prize-winning British author [[Kazuo Ishiguro]]. Narrated by Stevens, a butler at Darlington Hall near [[Oxford]], it follows his 1956 motoring trip to visit a former housekeeper in [[Cornwall]]. His memories of serving Lord Darlington in the 1920s and 1930s reveal his devotion to professional dignity and his personal regrets. The novel won the [[Booker Prize]] in 1989. A 1993 film starring [[Anthony Hopkins]] and [[Emma Thompson]] was nominated for eight [[Academy Awards]].

headword: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
entry: 1798 poem by English poet [[Samuel Taylor Coleridge]], first published in *Lyrical Ballads*, a collaboration with [[William Wordsworth]]. An old sailor stops a wedding guest to tell of a voyage in which his ship is driven south to icy Antarctic waters. He shoots an [[Albatross|albatross]] that had led the ship out of the ice, and his crew suffers and dies under a supernatural curse. The mariner survives and is redeemed when he blesses sea creatures. The poem is written in seven parts in ballad stanzas with archaic language. It is Coleridge's longest major poem and is often considered a signal shift to modern poetry. Some modern editions use a revised 1817 version with a gloss.

1913 ballet and orchestral concert work by [[Igor Stravinsky]]. Written for Sergei Diaghilev's Ballets Russes, its [[Avant-garde|avant-garde]] music and choreography by [[Vaslav Nijinsky]] caused a sensation at the premiere in Paris on May 29, 1913. The scenario depicts primitive rituals celebrating spring, in which a young girl is chosen as a sacrificial victim and dances herself to death. Stravinsky's score contains experiments in tonality, meter, rhythm and dissonance, and analysts have noted its grounding in Russian folk music. Nijinsky's original choreography, long believed lost, was reconstructed by the Joffrey Ballet in Los Angeles in the 1980s. The music is one of the most recorded works in the classical repertoire.

2006 post-apocalyptic novel by American writer [[Cormac McCarthy]]. A father and his young son journey on foot toward the sea across an ash-covered United States after an unspecified cataclysm has destroyed civilization and nearly all life. Their struggle to survive involves marauders, starvation and cannibalism. McCarthy's sparse style omits quotation marks. The novel won the [[Pulitzer Prize]] for Fiction in 2007 and was adapted into a 2009 film directed by John Hillcoat.

1975 musical comedy horror film directed by Jim Sharman, based on the 1973 stage musical *The Rocky Horror Show*. It parodies 1930s to early 1960s science-fiction and horror B movies. [[Susan Sarandon]] co-stars with Tim Curry, in his film debut. Beginning with midnight screenings at the Waverly Theater in [[New York City]] in 1976, audiences began to shout back at the screen and dress as the characters, creating shadow casts. The film is usually shown close to [[Halloween]]. It is the longest-running theatrical release in film history. In 2005 the [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the National Film Registry.

English rock band formed in [[London]] in 1962. Rooted in [[Blues|blues]], the band was at the forefront of the British Invasion and pioneered the gritty sound of hard rock. Mick Jagger and Keith Richards became its core songwriting partnership. Their songs "(I Can't Get No) Satisfaction" and "Paint It Black" became international number one hits in 1965 and 1966. Brian Jones, who named the band after a Muddy Waters song, left weeks before his death in 1969. *Sticky Fingers* (1971) was the first of eight consecutive number-one studio albums in the U.S. The Stones were inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1989 and have won four Grammy Awards.

Fresco by the Italian Renaissance artist [[Raphael]], painted between 1509 and 1511. It was commissioned by [[Pope Julius II]] for rooms in the Apostolic Palace in [[Vatican City]]. The fresco depicts an imagined assembly of ancient philosophers, mathematicians and scientists, with [[Plato]] and [[Aristotle]] at the center. Among the figures commonly identified are Socrates, Pythagoras, Archimedes, Euclid and Heraclitus. [[Leonardo da Vinci]] is believed to be portrayed as Plato and [[Michelangelo]] as Heraclitus. Raphael included a self-portrait beside Ptolemy. The figure in the white robe on the left, the only one to gaze at the viewer, is most commonly identified as Hypatia. The painting uses accurate [[Perspective (graphical)|perspective]] projection, a defining characteristic of Renaissance art.
